notes: Slot 18 = Velasco's Revolutionary Government of the Armed Forces (ruling). Coalition slot 19 holds the Maoist PCP-Bandera Roja, which is not a real partner; the pro-Soviet PCP (slot 4) gave the regime critical support. Slot 22 = the armed forces as an institution (MD sprite), distinct from the regime organization in 18. MD's AP placement in slot 1 and APRA in slot 3 kept. Patria Roja sprite not used because the pro-Soviet PCP takes slot 4.

0.name: Marina de Guerra del Perú
0.text:
The Peruvian Navy is the most conservative and most American-trained of the three services. Its admirals sit in Velasco's cabinet and junta, but the officer corps, drawn heavily from Lima's upper and middle classes, watches the expropriation of the International Petroleum Company and the agrarian reform with growing unease.

The navy's leadership stands for order, private property and close cooperation with the United States, and it distrusts the radical colonels around the president. Its leverage lies in its vote within the military government and in Callao, the country's main port and naval base, which no regime in Lima can ignore.

1.name: Acción Popular
1.text:
Popular Action was founded in 1956 by the architect Fernando Belaúnde Terry, who won the presidency in 1963 and was deposed by the army on 3 October 1968. Belaúnde lives in exile in the United States, party activity is suspended, and the movement is weakened by the split between his loyalists and the faction of Edgardo Seoane.

The party combines developmentalism, road building into the Amazon, cooperative 'Cooperación Popular' self-help and constitutional government. It is friendly to Washington and foreign investment. Its strength lies in the urban middle classes, the provinces it connected by highway, and the claim to be the last elected government of Peru.

2.name: Partido Demócrata Cristiano
2.text:
The Christian Democrat Party was founded in 1956 and split in 1966, when its conservative wing left to form the Christian People's Party. What remains is a small progressive party led by the jurist Héctor Cornejo Chávez, who has become one of the most prominent civilian supporters of the military government.

The party preaches communitarian reform inspired by Catholic social teaching: land to the tiller, worker participation in industry and independence from both superpowers. Its base is narrow, mostly Arequipa and Lima professionals, but its lawyers and intellectuals help draft the regime's reforms and lend it a civilian, Christian face.

3.name: Alianza Popular Revolucionaria Americana
3.text:
The American Popular Revolutionary Alliance, founded by Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre in 1924, is Peru's oldest and best organized mass party. The 1968 coup was staged partly to keep Haya from winning the 1969 elections; party life is now frozen, though the Apristas keep their 'Casa del Pueblo' and their unions.

Once anti-imperialist, APRA has moved toward moderate, anti-communist social democracy and accommodation with the United States. Its disciplined cadres dominate the north coast, the sugar estates of La Libertad and the Confederation of Workers of Peru. The military's reforms steal its programme while denying it power, and the old feud with the army endures.

4.name: Partido Comunista Peruano
4.text:
The Peruvian Communist Party, heir to José Carlos Mariátegui's Socialist Party of 1928, is the pro-Soviet rump left after the Maoists broke away in 1964. Led by Jorge del Prado, it is known by its newspaper 'Unidad' and operates semi-legally under the military government.

The party judges Velasco's regime anti-imperialist and offers it critical support, applauding the oil nationalization, the agrarian reform and new relations with Moscow. Its strength lies in the General Confederation of Workers of Peru, refounded under communist leadership in 1968, among miners, bank employees and teachers, and in its ties to the Soviet embassy.

5.name: Vanguardia Revolucionaria
5.text:
Revolutionary Vanguard was founded in 1965 by young intellectuals and former Apristas and Christian Democrats, among them Ricardo Letts Colmenares. It sits among a cluster of New Left groups that survived the crushing of the 1965 guerrillas of the Revolutionary Left Movement, and it works underground and in the universities.

The Vanguard rejects both Moscow's line and the military's 'revolution from above', calling Velasco's reforms a bourgeois manoeuvre. It organizes peasant federations and student unions, especially in Cusco and Lima, and dreams of a worker-peasant uprising. Its weight lies in the student movement and among the peasants who seized land before the reform.

6.name: Frente Nacional de Defensa del Petróleo
6.english: National Front for the Defence of Petroleum
6.native_full: Frente Nacional de Defensa del Petróleo
6.text:
The National Front for the Defence of Petroleum grew out of the long campaign against the International Petroleum Company and its La Brea y Pariñas oilfields. Bringing together nationalist officers, lawyers, journalists and intellectuals, it saw its cause triumph when the army seized the fields six days after the 1968 coup.

The front is fiercely anti-American and treats foreign capital as a threat to sovereignty. It wants state control of oil, mining and fishmeal, no compensation for the IPC and resistance to the Hickenlooper sanctions threatened by Washington. Its influence runs through the press and the military's nationalist officers rather than through a mass membership.

7.name: Comité de Asesoramiento de la Presidencia
7.native_full: Comité de Asesoramiento de la Presidencia
7.text:
The Presidential Advisory Committee is the brain trust of the military regime, staffed by the colonels who planned the 1968 coup under the code name 'Plan Inca'. Officers such as Leonidas Rodríguez Figueroa and Jorge Fernández Maldonado, the minister of energy and mines, form the radical core around Velasco.

The colonels want to break the oligarchy, nationalize strategic industries and steer Peru away from dependence on the United States, buying Soviet weapons if necessary. They draft the decrees, vet ministers and set the pace of reform. Their power rests entirely on Velasco's trust and their grip on the army's intelligence and planning staffs.

8.name: Amigos del Imam Sadr
8.text:
A handful of Lebanese Shia traders in Lima and the northern ports follow the rise of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who in 1969 became head of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut. They meet in shops and private homes, far from any mosque.

The circle wants dignity and representation for the Shia of south Lebanon and sends remittances home. It is politically cautious, loyal to whatever government grants it residence and trade, and suspicious of both superpowers. Its only leverage is commerce and a network of family ties stretching from Lima to Tyre and the Bekaa.

9.name: Lectores de Najaf
9.text:
The Readers of Najaf are a tiny cluster of Shia immigrants who pass around the sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf, where he has just lectured on government by the Islamic jurist. They have no premises and no legal existence in Peru.

They reject monarchy and secular nationalism alike and see both Washington and Moscow as arrogant powers. Their horizon is revolution in Iran rather than in the Andes. They have no influence in Peruvian politics beyond a few families, but they form the seed of a militant network should the wider Shia world ignite.

10.name: Los Amigos de Riad
10.text:
The Friends of Riyadh are a small group of Muslim merchants of Arab and South Asian origin in Lima who receive Korans, literature and occasional funds from the Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962. They pray together in rented rooms and hope for a proper mosque.

The circle teaches quietist, Saudi-approved Islam: obedience to rulers, avoidance of politics and staunch anti-communism. It looks with alarm at Velasco's opening to Moscow but keeps its head down. Its leverage is money from the Gulf and the respectability of well-established trading families in the capital.

11.name: Estudiantes del Califato
11.text:
The Students of the Caliphate are a few Arab and Pakistani students at Lima's universities who have encountered the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, Taqiuddin al-Nabhani's party for the restoration of the caliphate. They meet secretly and number no more than a dozen.

They regard every existing state, Muslim or not, as illegitimate and reject both capitalism and communism. Their programme is a single Islamic state under one caliph. In Peru they are a curiosity, but their discipline and conspiratorial habits mirror those of the radical left they meet on campus.

12.name: Los Hermanos del Rímac
12.text:
The Brothers of the Rímac are a small association of Palestinian and Syrian Muslim shopkeepers in Lima who admire the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood and Said Ramadan's exile network in Europe. They organize Koran lessons, charity and help for newcomers.

The circle favours Islamic ethics in public life, solidarity with the Palestinian cause and a cautious independence from both blocs. It respects the law of its host country and avoids open politics. Its strength is a tight community of traders and the textile and retail business they control in parts of the capital.

13.name: Centro de Altos Estudios Militares
13.text:
The Center for Higher Military Studies, founded in 1950 in Chorrillos, is the staff college where Peru's senior officers study economics, sociology and planning alongside civilian experts. Its doctrine of national security through development shaped the generation of officers who now run the state.

CAEM argues that poverty, the hacienda system and foreign dependence breed subversion, and that only a planned, technocratic state can secure the nation. It is neither pro-Soviet nor pro-American but nationalist and managerial. Its graduates fill the ministries and the National Planning Institute, giving it quiet influence over every reform.

14.name: Partido Popular Cristiano
14.text:
The Christian People's Party was founded in 1966 by Luis Bedoya Reyes, the popular former mayor of Lima, and other conservatives who left the Christian Democrat Party. Like all parties it has been sidelined by the military government.

The party defends private enterprise, the family, Catholic values and a return to constitutional rule, opposing the regime's statism and land reform. It draws on Lima's middle and upper classes, Catholic professionals and businessmen. Its leverage is Bedoya's personal popularity in the capital and its ties to the business associations alarmed by Velasco's reforms.

15.name: Sociedad Nacional Agraria
15.text:
The National Agrarian Society is the association of Peru's great landowners, the coastal sugar and cotton barons and the highland hacendados who dominated the republic for a century. The Agrarian Reform Law of June 1969 has already seized the great sugar estates of the north and turned them into cooperatives.

The society fights the reform in the courts and the press, demands compensation in cash rather than bonds and warns of communism. Its families still control banks, newspapers and export houses. Its leverage is money, foreign connections and a web of kinship reaching into the officer corps and the Church.

16.name: Sociedad Nacional de Industrias
16.text:
The National Society of Industries, founded in 1896, represents Peru's manufacturers, from Lima textile mills to food processors and fishmeal plants. In 1970 it faces a military government that is preparing a General Industries Law with state control of basic industry and worker profit-sharing.

The society stands for private enterprise, protection against imports but freedom from state interference, and foreign investment. It resists the 'industrial community' schemes being drafted by the colonels and lobbies quietly through ministries and banks. Its leverage is capital, employment and the regime's need for industrial growth.

17.name: Defensores de la Vicuña
17.text:
The Defenders of the Vicuña are the circle of naturalists, scientists and patrons around the conservationist Felipe Benavides Barreda, who campaigns to save the vicuña from poachers. The Pampa Galeras reserve in Ayacucho, created in 1967, is their great success.

They call for national parks, protection of the Amazon and the guano islands, and a ban on the vicuña wool trade, enlisting international support from the World Wildlife Fund. Their base is small and elite, but their access to ministers, the press and foreign conservation bodies gives them influence far beyond their numbers.

18.name: Gobierno Revolucionario de la Fuerza Armada
18.english: Revolutionary Government of the Armed Forces
18.native_full: Gobierno Revolucionario de la Fuerza Armada
18.text:
The Revolutionary Government of the Armed Forces seized power on 3 October 1968 under General Juan Velasco Alvarado. Within a year it nationalized the International Petroleum Company, decreed a sweeping agrarian reform and proclaimed a revolution that is 'neither capitalist nor communist'.

The regime pursues a third way of humanist, participatory socialism: expropriating the oligarchy, creating cooperatives, expanding the state and asserting sovereignty over 200 nautical miles of sea. It recognizes the Soviet Union, defies Washington and seeks a place among the non-aligned. Its power rests on the army, the officer corps' loyalty to Velasco and the hope it raises among peasants.
18.wiki: Revolutionary Government of the Armed Forces of Peru

19.name: Partido Comunista del Perú – Bandera Roja
19.english: Communist Party of Peru – Red Flag
19.native_full: Partido Comunista del Perú – Bandera Roja
19.text:
The Communist Party of Peru – Red Flag is the Maoist party born of the 1964 split with the pro-Soviet communists and led by the lawyer Saturnino Paredes. It is wracked by factional war: Patria Roja broke away in 1969, and the Ayacucho committee of Abimael Guzmán is about to go its own way.

The party calls Peru semi-feudal and semi-colonial and preaches protracted people's war from the countryside, following Peking. It denounces Velasco's regime as fascist. Its strength lies in peasant federations, the teachers' movement and the University of Huamanga, where Maoism has struck deep roots.

20.name: Unión Nacional Odriísta
20.text:
The Odriist National Union was founded in 1961 as the vehicle of General Manuel Odría, dictator from 1948 to 1956. Allied with APRA in Congress against Belaúnde in the late 1960s, it has been pushed aside by the 1968 coup, and its ageing leader remains its only real programme.

Odriísmo mixes authoritarian order, anti-communism and populist paternalism, remembered for public works, schools and gifts to the shantytowns of Lima. It is friendly to the United States and hostile to the radical colonels. Its base lies in the barriadas and among nostalgic officers and provincial notables.

21.name: Unión Revolucionaria
21.text:
The Revolutionary Union was founded in 1931 as the party of President Luis Miguel Sánchez Cerro and turned openly fascist under Luis A. Flores in the 1930s, with blackshirt militias and corporatist doctrine. By 1970 it is a small remnant that still contests a place on the far right.

The party preaches Catholic corporatism, hierarchy, mestizo nationalism and implacable hostility to APRA and communism. It admires Franco's Spain. Its influence is marginal, limited to old veterans of the 1930s and some conservative officers, but its slogans of order and nation still find listeners in times of crisis.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas del Perú
22.text:
The Armed Forces of Peru, the army, navy and air force under their Joint Command, are the institution behind the 1968 coup. Beyond Velasco's inner circle, the officer corps remains a professional and hierarchical body with its own interests and rivalries.

The institution values order, unity of command, modern equipment and the honour of the uniform above any ideology. Most commanders back the reforms as long as they serve national security, but many fear radicalism and civilian mobilization. As the ultimate arbiter of Peruvian politics, the armed forces can sustain the revolution or end it.

23.name: Círculo Virreinal
23.text:
The Viceregal Circle gathers Lima aristocrats of old Spanish lineage, holders of colonial titles of Castile and admirers of Franco's plans to restore the Spanish crown. They meet in clubs and mansions where the memory of the Viceroyalty of Peru is cultivated.

The circle dreams of a Catholic, hierarchical order under a monarch tied to the Spanish Bourbons, and despises both the military reformers and the parties. It has no popular base whatsoever. Its only assets are wealth, social prestige and the land and houses the agrarian reform is now taking away.
